title: Bulkhead
summary: A bulkhead isolates resources so a failure in one part of the system doesn't take down everything else. Like watertight compartments in a ship's hull, if one compartment floods, the ship stays afloat. In software: separate thread pools, connection pools, or processes for different services or workloads.
why_it_matters: Without bulkheads, all your services share the same thread pool and connection pool. One slow downstream service consumes all threads, and your service can't handle requests for other (healthy) downstreams. Bulkheads isolate failures so only the affected part of the system degrades.

payload.text:
The name comes from ship design: a ship's hull is divided into watertight compartments (bulkheads). If one compartment floods, the door is closed and the ship stays afloat. The damage is isolated.

In software, the same principle applies: if your service calls 3 downstream services (A, B, C), and they all share one thread pool, a failure in A can consume all threads and prevent B and C from being served. A bulkhead gives each downstream its own pool — A's failure only affects A's pool.

payload.caption: Without bulkheads, one slow service starves everything. With bulkheads, each service is isolated.
payload.alt_text: Two diagrams. Without a bulkhead: all three downstream services share one pool of 100 threads. When service A becomes slow, it consumes all 100 threads, and services B and C are starved — the entire service is down. With a bulkhead: each service has its own pool (30 for A, 30 for B, 40 for C). When service A saturates its pool, only A is degraded — services B and C continue working normally.

payload.text:
Bulkheads can be implemented at different levels:

- **Thread pools**: separate pool per downstream service. Most common.
- **Connection pools**: separate HTTP/TCP connection pool per downstream.
- **Processes**: separate processes (or containers) per service type. Strongest isolation.
- **Machines**: separate servers per workload. Physical isolation.

The stronger the isolation, the more resource-expensive. Thread pools are the sweet spot for most cases.

payload.title: Bulkhead + Circuit Breaker
payload.body: Bulkheads limit the blast radius. Circuit breakers stop calling a failing service entirely. Together: the circuit breaker prevents new calls to a failing service, and the bulkhead ensures that even if the breaker is slow to trip, other services aren't affected. This combination is the foundation of resilient microservice architecture.

payload.question: Your service has a single thread pool of 200 threads and calls 3 downstream services. One downstream starts responding slowly. What happens without a bulkhead?
options: Only requests to the slow downstream are affected.
The slow downstream consumes all 200 threads, and requests to the other two downstreams also fail.
The service automatically scales up more threads.
Nothing — 200 threads is enough for anyone.
payload.rationale: Without a bulkhead, all three downstreams share the same 200-thread pool. The slow downstream causes each of its requests to hold a thread for longer (waiting for the slow response). As more requests come in, all 200 threads eventually get consumed by the slow downstream, leaving no threads for the other two — they fail too, even though they're healthy. This is why bulkheads (separate thread pools per downstream) are essential in resilient architecture.

payload.question: What is the relationship between bulkheads and circuit breakers?
options: They are the same thing — different names for one pattern.
Bulkheads limit the blast radius; circuit breakers stop calling a failing service entirely. They complement each other.
Circuit breakers replace bulkheads — you only need one.
Bulkheads replace circuit breakers.
payload.rationale: Bulkheads and circuit breakers are complementary, not alternatives. A bulkhead limits the blast radius of a failure — if one downstream is slow, only its thread pool is affected, not the others. A circuit breaker stops calling a failing service entirely — it 'trips open' after enough failures. Together: the breaker prevents new calls, and the bulkhead ensures that even before the breaker trips, other services aren't starved. Most resilient systems use both.

payload.text: **Mental model.** Think of Bulkhead as a deliberate boundary in a system. The boundary exists because something becomes harder to manage when everything is done in one place: latency, scale, failure isolation, consistency, cost, or team ownership. The useful question is not “what does Bulkhead mean?” but “what pressure makes this boundary worth introducing, and what new failure mode does it create?”

payload.title: Design lens
payload.body: Before choosing Bulkhead, name the workload, the critical user path, the dominant bottleneck, the failure you are trying to absorb, and the trade-off you are willing to accept. If you cannot name those five things, the design is probably premature.

payload.title: Hint
payload.body: If you are stuck on Bulkhead, start by drawing the request path and marking every network hop, stateful component, queue, cache and failure boundary. Then estimate where the system will saturate.

payload.question: You increase traffic by 10× in a system using Bulkhead. What should you inspect first?
options: The newest framework version
The dominant bottleneck and its saturation signal
Only the UI
Nothing; the architecture should absorb any traffic automatically
payload.rationale: System design is a constraint-and-bottleneck exercise. Start with the resource or dependency that will saturate first, then choose the smallest change that removes that bottleneck.

payload.question: Which statement is the safest engineering habit when using Bulkhead?
options: Choose it because it is popular
Add it before measuring the problem
State the workload, failure mode and trade-off it is solving
Use the most distributed design possible
payload.rationale: Good architecture starts from requirements, workload and failure assumptions. The component is the consequence of that reasoning, not the starting point.

payload.prompt: Production scenario: your system uses Bulkhead, traffic suddenly spikes, and p99 latency doubles. What is your first move?
payload.context: You have dashboards for traffic, latency, errors and saturation. You can change the architecture, but every change has operational cost.

options.outcome: This may help, but only if compute saturation is the bottleneck.

options.text: Inspect the bottleneck and its saturation signal first
options.outcome: Correct: diagnose before scaling or introducing a new pattern.
This removes the evidence you need to diagnose the incident.

payload.rationale: Measure the limiting resource or dependency first. A bottleneck can be compute, database I/O, network, cache misses, lock contention, downstream latency, or queue backlog.

payload.text: **Answer this without notes:** When would you choose Bulkhead, and when would you intentionally avoid it? Mention at least one bottleneck it addresses, one failure mode it introduces, and one alternative. Then quantify the workload you are designing for.

payload.title: Engineering lens
payload.body: For Bulkhead, treat the system as a control loop: observe load and failure, choose a bounded response, and measure whether the response stabilizes the system instead of simply moving the bottleneck somewhere else.

payload.text:
### Numerical sanity check

When estimating capacity, distinguish average from peak. If average traffic is 4,000 RPS and the observed peak-to-average factor is 3×, design the first pass around roughly 12,000 RPS, then leave headroom for failure and growth.

payload.question: What is the earliest signal that Bulkhead is becoming the bottleneck: latency, saturation, errors, queue depth, or something else? Why?
payload.context: Do not optimize for a memorized definition. Reason from the workload and failure mode.
options: Scale the same component immediately.
Measure the current bottleneck and state the assumption that changed.
Add more technologies until throughput improves.
Choose the most popular architecture.
payload.rationale: Good system design starts with the bottleneck and the changed constraint. The most popular or complex choice is not automatically correct.

pros: Isolates failures — one broken downstream doesn't take down everything.
Allows partial degradation — some features work while others fail.
Composable with circuit breakers for layered resilience.
cons: More resource overhead — separate pools means more idle threads.
Harder to tune — how big should each pool be?
Adds complexity — more moving parts to monitor and debug.
Can cause under-utilization — if one pool is idle while another is saturated, you can't borrow.

failure_modes: Pool too small — legitimate traffic gets rejected even when the downstream is healthy.
Pool too large — too many concurrent calls overwhelm the downstream.
No monitoring — if you don't know a pool is saturated, you can't diagnose the failure.
common_mistakes: Using a single shared pool for all downstreams — defeats the purpose.
Making pools too small — causes false failures under normal load spikes.
Forgetting to monitor pool utilization — you need to know when pools are near saturation.

Configures per-upstream connection pools and circuit breakers at the sidecar, isolating failures without application code changes.
